pacer.summary: A learned eviction policy for LLM prefix (KV) caches, tested against tuned heuristics on held-out public traces.
pacer.card: Learned eviction for LLM prefix caches, tested in simulation on public traces.
pacer.role: Solo research project: design, code, experiments and write-up
pacer.status: Research prototype. Trace-driven simulation, not a production deployment.

cover.alt: Bar chart of block hit ratio on the chat trace at four cache sizes, comparing LRU, ATC'25, Pacer and the offline references.

stat.label: test cells ahead of the best tuned heuristic
stat.source: Held-out hour, four public Qwen traces × four cache sizes. Simulation.

pacer.problem: LLM servers can reuse the work behind a repeated prompt prefix. When the cache fills, choosing the wrong block to discard means doing that work again. I wanted to test whether predicting reuse could improve on simple eviction rules without making the eviction path expensive.
pacer.built: A learned eviction policy and the experiment around it. A small LightGBM model estimates whether a cached block will be reused soon, and the policy evicts the sampled block least likely to return. I replayed four public Alibaba Qwen traces through an event-driven simulator and compared the policy with tuned heuristics on an hour of traffic it had never seen.

parts.title: Replay real traffic
parts.body: Four public Alibaba Qwen traces supply chat, API, coding and reasoning traffic. The event-driven simulator keeps active requests' blocks pinned and evicts only unused leaves, preserving valid prompt prefixes.

parts.title: Learn a useful question
parts.body: A small LightGBM model estimates whether a block will be reused soon, given how long it has already been idle. Training examples do not depend on a particular cache size. Each workload gets its own model.

parts.title: Keep the decision cheap
parts.body: The fixed policy samples 32 evictable blocks and removes the one least likely to return. It follows matching parent history and reuses one scored sample for up to four evictions in a burst. The model runs in Rust.

parts.title: Check two kinds of reality
parts.body: The Python reference checks the Rust simulator's behavior. Held-out traces test policy quality. A separate laptop replay uses a real MLX KV pool to check whether a better simulated hit ratio produces a latency benefit.

pacer.contribution: This is my solo research project. I built the Rust simulator and its eviction policies, a Python reference implementation, the LightGBM training and evaluation pipeline, and the MLX replay that connects the same Rust controller to a real KV pool through PyO3.

media.alt: Terminal recording of Pacer's make demo command
media.caption: `make demo`, in real time: five policies on the held-out hour of the chat trace. About 39 seconds, most of it one slow baseline.

media.alt: Four line charts of block hit ratio against cache size, one per trace. Pacer sits at or above the best tuned heuristic in each and below the Belady offline reference.
media.caption: Block hit ratio on the held-out hour, for each trace and cache size. Simulation. Drawn by the repo's own `make figures` from committed results.

decisions.title: A difficult baseline
decisions.choice: I tune baseline settings on validation data, then compare with the best heuristic for each test cell, selected with hindsight.
decisions.tradeoff: It gives the comparison an advantage over Pacer, but prevents a weak default setting from making the result look impressive.

decisions.title: Workload-specific learning
decisions.choice: I train on minutes 0–45, choose settings on minutes 45–60 and report the second hour. Every additional look at the test hour is logged.
decisions.tradeoff: This is one temporal split per trace. Models do not reliably transfer between workloads, so the result is narrower than a universal cache policy.

decisions.title: Hits are not all equally valuable
decisions.choice: The main policy predicts reuse. I also tested scoring candidates by expected saved compute.
decisions.tradeoff: Improving block hit ratio does not guarantee the most compute saved: deep prompt blocks cost more to rebuild. On chat at 2–10% cache, the main policy trails ATC'25 in compute saved.

pacer.lesson: The interesting result is not that ML wins everywhere. A small model improves 13 of 16 measured cells, and the remaining headroom shows what the available metadata cannot predict. These are simulated hit ratios, not a production result: the separate laptop replay showed only a 1.2% lower mean time to first token than LRU.

tilelens.summary: A local vision-and-search tool that reads a tile game from the screen and draws its best plays back over it.
tilelens.card: Reads a tile game off the screen and overlays the best word plays, locally.
tilelens.role: Solo project: design, code, tests and measurements
tilelens.status: Working side project on one Apple-silicon Mac. Not for ranked play.

cover.alt: TileLens drawing a suggested play as ghost tiles over a live Letter League game, with its panel listing the top three plays.

stat.label: median move search
stat.source: Mid-game 13×13 boards, 204k-word list. Measures search, not the whole screen-to-overlay loop.

tilelens.problem: A useful overlay has to read letters, point values and board geometry while the game is moving. One uncertain tile can corrupt an otherwise exact search. I wanted fast suggestions that stay attached to the actual on-screen position.
tilelens.built: A tool that watches the screen, finds and reads the board, waits for a position it can trust, searches every legal placement and previews the best play as ghost tiles over the game. Frames stay in memory on the machine, with no cloud model and no network requests at run time. The hard part is knowing when not to trust the pixels.

parts.title: Read only what changed
parts.body: Capture runs at about 10 Hz. Unchanged frames skip recognition. Board colors locate the grid, and a movement immediately clears the preview so a suggestion cannot drift away from its board.

parts.title: Make uncertainty visible
parts.body: A position must agree across three frames. Remembered tiles and word-list constraints help settle unclear letters. Unresolved squares become walls for search, and the panel exposes possible corrections.

parts.title: Search independently
parts.body: A directed word graph searches legal placements in a separate process and keeps the top three by this turn's score. An independent brute-force solver checks the fast implementation on seeded positions.

parts.title: Draw without interfering
parts.body: A click-through overlay draws ghost tiles and never places them. Its own windows are excluded from capture. Search results are accepted only while the board still matches the position that produced them.

tilelens.contribution: I built the complete system: screen capture and change detection, board alignment, letter and value recognition, the settle step, the DAWG move generator, the PySide6 panel and overlay, a synthetic game for testing, and the benchmarks.

media.alt: Recording of TileLens over a live Letter League game in Discord
media.caption: A live Letter League game in Discord, recorded on November 11, 2026. About 50 seconds, real time. Player card blurred.

media.alt: Recording of TileLens in demo mode with its built-in synthetic game
media.caption: The app in demo mode, playing its built-in synthetic game. 58 seconds.

decisions.title: Correctness before coverage
decisions.choice: I flag unresolved tiles and let search work around them instead of silently choosing a letter.
decisions.tradeoff: A valid play can be missed until the uncertainty is resolved. The word list can also disagree with the game's dictionary.

decisions.title: One turn, done well
decisions.choice: The search maximizes the current turn's score and explicitly labels an interrupted search as best found so far.
decisions.tradeoff: It does not model opponents, future turns or the strategic value of keeping particular rack tiles.

decisions.title: A local native overlay
decisions.choice: Screen frames stay in memory, with no cloud model or runtime network requests.
decisions.tradeoff: Capture and window behavior were tested on one Apple-silicon Mac. Other platforms and real-game conditions have much less coverage.

tilelens.lesson: The 2.2 ms median measures move search on mid-game 13×13 boards, not the entire screen-to-overlay loop. The more important engineering result is that stale or uncertain input does not quietly become a confident suggestion.

classmap.summary: A campus app that turns a UC Santa Cruz class schedule into rooms you can find, plus a separate web map with walking routes.
classmap.card: A UCSC class schedule on a campus map, plus a separate web map with routes.
classmap.role: Solo project: design, code, data pipeline and tests
classmap.status: Working app and web map. Tested in the iOS Simulator; not on an app store.

links.label: Open the web map
links.note: The build from the repo. Loads map tiles from OpenFreeMap.

cover.alt: The Classmap web map showing a walking route from Kresge College to Jack Baskin Engineering.

stat.label: official classrooms resolve
stat.source: UCSC's general-assignment classrooms, each to a building, room and position. Name resolution, not a survey of physical doors.

classmap.problem: A schedule can say “Baskin Engr 152” without explaining where that room is. General map apps often stop at a building name. I wanted one place to import a schedule, see today's classes and resolve UCSC room names, including abbreviations and typos.
classmap.built: Two separate interfaces over the same campus data. The Flutter app imports a class schedule, shows the day's classes and resolves each room name to a building, room and position. The web map, built with React and MapLibre, explores campus places and computes walking routes in the browser.

parts.title: Ship the campus with the app
parts.body: Building, room, alias and calendar data are bundled assets. Search and the saved schedule work offline without an app server or account. Map imagery still comes from an external tile provider.

parts.title: Import without a cloud round trip
parts.body: Schedules can be pasted, imported from an .ics file or entered by hand. On iOS, Apple's Vision framework reads a schedule image on the device before Dart code turns the text into classes for review.

parts.title: Port behavior, not just code
parts.body: The Dart search, schedule reader and calendar reader are checked against recorded outputs from the original Python implementation. A separate check keeps the app's bundled data in sync with the source data.

parts.title: Two interfaces, distinct jobs
parts.body: The phone app sends a destination to Apple Maps or Google Maps for walking directions. The separate web map explores campus places and computes routes over the OpenStreetMap path network in the browser.

classmap.contribution: I built the Flutter app, the Dart search and schedule parsers, calendar and on-device photo import, class reminders, the Python campus-data pipeline, and the React/MapLibre web map. The web map includes Dijkstra routing with slope-aware walking-time estimates.

media.alt: Recording of the Classmap app in the iOS Simulator
media.caption: The app in the iOS Simulator with an invented schedule. Real time, 49 seconds.

media.alt: Recording of the Classmap web map searching for places and drawing a walking route
media.caption: The web map, served locally and recorded in headless Chrome. 29 seconds.

decisions.title: Offline data needs upkeep
decisions.choice: I bundle room search and keep the schedule on the phone.
decisions.tradeoff: Campus data and term dates need explicit updates. Offline search does not promise offline map imagery.

decisions.title: Hand off navigation
decisions.choice: The phone app passes the room destination to the system maps app instead of rebuilding turn-by-turn navigation.
decisions.tradeoff: It relies on another app for the walk and does not provide indoor floor guidance. Unknown rooms fall back to their building's main door.

decisions.title: Be precise about verification
decisions.choice: I tested the app in the iOS Simulator and checked every official general-assignment classroom name.
decisions.tradeoff: The 87/87 result is name resolution, not a physical survey of every door. Real-device notification delivery and photo import on real photos remain unverified; the app is not in an app store.

classmap.lesson: The technically interesting part is the seam between messy schedule text and reliable campus data: a behavior-checked Dart port, on-device import and a useful offline core. The app and web map are separate working interfaces, with separate limits.

ethocal.summary: A team Flutter app for sustainable shopping. The concept won the DesignVerse Hackathon at UC Riverside in May 2026.
ethocal.card: A team app for sustainable shopping. I built its messaging, profile and event pages.
ethocal.role: Team member. I built four parts of the interface.
ethocal.status: In development with the team. Private repository.
ethocal.sealed: Private team repository. No public captures.
ethocal.problem: Ethocal is a thrifting and marketplace app meant to fight fast fashion. It puts ethical brands, thrift stores, yard sales and events in one place.
ethocal.built: The idea started at the DesignVerse Hackathon at UC Riverside in May 2026, where our team of five won with the concept. The team has been developing it as a Flutter app since, using Riverpod, the repository pattern and Dio, with flows and wireframes in Figma and FigJam.
ethocal.contribution: I built the messaging interface, the profile pages, the schedule and edit-event pages, and the event details page. The rest of the app is my teammates' work.
ethocal.contributionNote: This list is my own account of my part. The repository is private and belongs to a teammate, so it cannot be checked from here.
